sections.h2: Who sends the Tyler tax statement
sections.html:
Billing and collection for every local taxing unit in Smith County, Tyler included, runs through one office: the Smith County tax office, 1517 W. Front St., Tyler, TX 75702. Mail goes to P.O. Box 2011 and the phone is (903) 590-2920. The doors are open from 8 a.m. until half past four, and the lunch hour is included.

One Tyler bill can carry several lines: the city, Smith County, Tyler Junior College and a school district. The school district depends on your address, because some Tyler properties sit in Whitehouse ISD or Chapel Hill ISD instead of Tyler ISD.

For 2026-2027 the city rate is $0.242063, the Smith County rate is $0.374088, Tyler Junior College is $0.210312 and Tyler ISD is $0.835000. Smith County's rate table shows the same figures as adopted rates for tax year 2026.

Tyler addresses served by other districts pay different school rates: Whitehouse ISD is 0.964900 and Chapel Hill ISD is 1.072900 for 2026. For the precise rate on your own parcel, ask the county office.

Since the mid 1990s the city has trimmed its rate by over half. It was $0.5336 in 1994-95 and reached a low of $0.1990 in 2007-08. The rate then rose to $0.2699 in 2021-22 before dropping each year to $0.236452 in 2025-26.

The 2026-27 rate of $0.242063 is higher than last year's and above the city's no-new-revenue rate of 0.232965. The city also continues to commit two cents of its rate to the street fund, equal to $2.4 million.

  • 1994-95: $0.5336
  • 2007-08: $0.1990
  • 2021-22: $0.2699
  • 2025-26: $0.236452
  • 2026-27: $0.242063

Most Tyler-area lines fell from 2022 to 2026, while the county's rose.

  • Smith County: 0.330000 in 2022, 0.347264 in 2023, 0.364231 in 2024 and 2025, then 0.374088 in 2026.
  • Tyler ISD: 1.179300 in 2022, 0.960000 in 2023, 0.910000 in 2024, 0.845000 in 2025 and 0.835000 in 2026.
  • Tyler Junior College: 0.188001 in 2022, then 0.185068 in 2025 and 0.210312 in 2026.
  • City of Tyler: 0.261850 in 2022 and 0.242063 in 2026.

The statement you receive is the final word on your exact figure.

Sales tax in Tyler is 8.25 percent. The state takes 6.25 percent, the city's general fund 1 percent, Tyler's One Half Cent Sales Tax Corporation 0.5 percent and Smith County 0.5 percent.

If the house ever hosted overnight guests, occupancy taxes were due through the city's portal at tylertx.hdlgov.com. The finance department can say whether any balance remains, so ask before you list.

Tyler's population reached 113,723 in mid 2025, a 7.4 percent gain on 2020. Owner-occupied homes have a midpoint value of $235,300, and 55.4 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Rent has a median of $1,252 a month, while owning costs $1,743 with a loan and $664 without.

Bills go out near October 1. You may pay as soon as one arrives, and no penalty applies until after January 31. Anything still open on February 1 counts as delinquent.

Lateness costs a 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest at the start. Each following month adds a point of penalty until it stops at 12 percent on July 1, and interest runs at a point a month with no stop. Collection attorneys hired by a unit may charge up to 20 percent more. A two-payment plan exists for some homeowners, with half due November 30 and the rest June 30 of the next year. Ask the Smith County office if you qualify.

Each school district must exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value. Owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, receive $60,000 beyond that on the school district value. Most exemption filings are due at the appraisal district before May 1.

Other state-level protections apply to Tyler homes too:

  • A residence homestead's appraised value cannot climb faster than 10 percent a year once you have qualified for a year.
  • A school-tax ceiling protects seniors and disabled owners and moves with them to another Texas homestead.
  • A disabled veteran receives $5,000, $7,500, $10,000 or $12,000 depending on rating, and one rated 100 percent disabled is fully exempt on the homestead.

Cities, counties and colleges may adopt local exemptions. Ask the Smith County Appraisal District for the current local percentages.

File a protest with the appraisal review board by May 15, or within 30 days after you get your notice if that comes later. Homestead notices land near April 1, and hearings start around mid May.

After a ruling you dislike, three paths remain: district court, binding arbitration, or a SOAH hearing when the board value tops $1,000,000. An appeal never pauses the bill, so pay at least the undisputed amount before it goes delinquent.

sections.h2: Taxes when you sell a Tyler house
sections.html:
Each year's tax lien forms on January 1, and whoever owns the house on that day answers for the year's tax. Your sale contract assigns the shares at closing.

If you sell during the year, request the balance due from the Smith County Tax Office in writing before closing. Your homestead exemption stays behind when you leave. If you never filed, the buyer can apply for the rest of that year after a closing past January 1, and heirs lacking a recorded deed submit an ownership affidavit with the death certificate.

Back taxes will not stop you from selling. At closing the title company settles them out of your proceeds, and a cash buyer need not wait on a bank's appraisal. Collect your newest statement, request a payoff, and confirm which school district your parcel falls in so you can walk a buyer through the bill.

sections.h2: A short checklist for Tyler sellers
sections.html:
Tyler bills stack four or five separate lines, so a buyer will want to see them broken out. Before you talk to anyone about price, work down this list.

  1. Find the tax statement and circle the school district line.
  2. Phone the county office on W. Front St. and ask for a payoff good through your expected closing date.
  3. Check that a homestead exemption is on file, and ask the appraisal district what local exemptions apply.
  4. Note whether you protested last spring and whether the appeal is still open.
  5. Tell the title company about any short-term rental use, since occupancy tax belongs to the city rather than the county.

Having these answers in one folder helps whether you list the house or sell it for cash.

faqs.q: What is the City of Tyler property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city rate is $0.242063 for 2026-2027, the same as the adopted 2026 figure in Smith County's table. Your full bill also includes county, junior college and school district rates.

faqs.q: Where do Tyler homeowners pay their tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Smith County Tax Office at 1517 W. Front St., Tyler, or call (903) 590-2920. The county office collects for all taxing jurisdictions in Smith County, including the City of Tyler.

faqs.q: When do Tyler property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: February 1 for most bills. Payment is due by January 31, and unpaid tax on February 1 picks up a 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest.

faqs.q: Is every Tyler address in Tyler ISD?
faqs.a: No. Some properties inside Tyler are in Whitehouse ISD or Chapel Hill ISD. Check your tax statement to see which school district rate applies.

faqs.q: How much is the homestead exemption in Tyler?
faqs.a: School districts must give $140,000 off a residence homestead's value, plus $60,000 more for seniors or disabled owners. Ask the Smith County Appraisal District about local exemption amounts for the city and county.
